title: Childhood lead poisoning: conservative estimates of the social and economic benefits of lead hazard control.
ehr_evidence: The estimated number of children affected in each group is a combination of two sets of data: pooled NHANES (2003–2006) and state child blood lead surveillance data from the National Center for Environmental Health (CDC 2007a).
summary: A cost–benefit analysis quantifying the social and economic benefits of household lead paint hazard control in a 2006 U.S. cohort of children ≤ 6 years of age, finding large returns on investment.
key_findings: Each dollar invested in lead paint hazard control returns $17–$221, with a net benefit of $181–$269 billion.
Total benefits of lead hazard control range from $192–$270 billion versus costs of $1.2–$11.0 billion.
After adjusting for other lead sources, net benefit ranges from $124–$188 billion, a return of $12–$155 per dollar invested.
Total IQ loss from elevated BLLs falls between 9.3 and 13.1 million points, with net lifetime earnings loss of $165–$233 billion.
Lead-linked crime direct costs total approximately $1.8 billion.
captured_features: number of children affected per BLL group
population: U.S. children ≤ 6 years of age (2006 cohort)
exposure_domain: heavy metals (lead exposure from lead-based paint)
limitations: Analysis restricted to lead-based paint as the only lead source, downwardly biasing cost estimates and inflating return on investment.
Uses conservative lower bounds of lead prevalence and excludes many costs (later-in-life health care, neonatal mortality, indirect crime costs, property value gains).
Small sample sizes prevent accurate categorization of children into BLL subgroups.
